He sucked one more shuddering breath and dove, black water swallowing him whole. It was so much worse the second time. His muscles were jelly, lungs scalded raw. Each stroke felt a half-second too slow. He swept his arms wide, blind, hands rasping pipe and plaster, mentally mapping the way back. The water pressure slammed into his body like a second impact, stealing the little air he had left. But he pushed through it, arms out, kicking hard. He followed the flow, felt for resistance. The movement was stronger now — more urgent, less controlled — and he knew what that meant. He'd been in enough trials to know what David panicking felt like. The movement thrashed ahead, strong, furious, off course. Dwight lunged, hand snagging something. Fabric. Arm. Elbow. The flail that followed would’ve knocked his teeth in if not for the drag of the water. He pulled. David pulled back on reflex, wrong direction, and Dwight held on and redirected, hand over hand up David's arm until he had him by the collar and could haul him bodily toward the ceiling. They surfaced together in a mess of limbs and swearing. David gasped like someone being born again, hair plastered to his face, arm curling tight against Dwight’s as they clawed for the edge. This time, it was David who found the lip, muscling them both up and over in a final, sodden scramble. They got out. That was the only thought Dwight's brain could hold for a while — the simple, enormous fact of tile under his hands and air above his head, real air, not a shrinking inch of it with water pressing in from below. He stayed down, pressed tight against solid ground, and coughed until his chest ached and then kept coughing anyway, because his lungs had opinions about the last several minutes and they were going to be heard. Somewhere beside him, David was doing the same. For a long, long moment, they didn’t move. Then David started laughing. For half a second, Dwight couldn’t tell if it was actually laughter or sobbing. His ears were still ringing from the silence below, and the sound scraped like a blade across bruised nerves. The deep hiccups of laughter broke the silence with a wheezing, exhausted lilt — helpless and a little broken at the edges and contagious in the specific way that delirious relief always was. Somehow, that made it real. They’d made it. Barely. Dwight answered with a grunt and flopped sideways on the cold tile, absolutely spent. “Next time,” David gasped through rawed-out chuckles, “you lead.” “Next time,” Dwight muttered, “I stay upstairs.” — THWACK. Dwight let out a sharp yelp of pain as something solid smacked into the side of his head. He blinked, vision swimming, catching a blur of movement and a sharp gasp and the scrape of boots on tile as whoever had hit him scrambled backward. A beam of light swung across them — strong and bright and absolutely blinding after hours of nothing — and Dwight threw an arm up against it, eyes watering. "Oh my god—" A voice. Female. Familiar. "Oh my god, I'm so sorry, I didn't see you, I almost—" David hissed and tried to turn away from the light, entirely too bright after all the darkness. The light veered quickly to one side with a trail of apologies, finally letting Dwight’s eyes adjust enough to see Orela — wild-eyed, nearly having walked straight into the hole they’d just escaped, were it not for the sudden human speed bump in the way. “Holy fuck,” Dwight choked, rubbing his eyes with a groan. “Warn a guy before kicking his brain back into his skull...” “Oh my god, I didn’t see you!” Orela stooped to help Dwight sit up. “We thought we heard something so I was just...how did you even get in here? What happened?” David coughed out another laugh. “Spent some time in the school’s new waterpark. I don’t recommend it.” Orela helped Dwight to sit upright, frowning as swept the flashlight over the two of them, taking in their state fully for the first time, soaked and wheezing on the floor. The beam passed over the hole and froze as realization sank in. “You guys were downstairs this whole time?” The three of them sat there, blinking in the flashlight glare, dripping onto the hallway floor as the silence of the preschool returned. Orela stared at the hole for a moment longer than was strictly necessary. The water lapped softly at its edges, dark and patient, like it was waiting to see if anyone else was going to come back for it. "Right," she said, in the tone of someone filing several things away to process later. She crouched down and got a hand under Dwight's arm, helping him upright. He came up slowly, waterlogged and unsteady. "Sorry about your head," she said. "S'fine," Dwight managed. It wasn't entirely fine. But it was fine enough. David got himself up without assistance through what appeared to be sheer principle, made it to vertical, and stayed there through an act of will that Orela clocked but didn't comment on. She cast one last look at the hole in the floor before turning away. The three of them moved off into the dark of the hallway, wet footsteps marking the tile behind them. Behind them, the water lapped quietly at the edge of the hole. Rising, still. Patient as anything. Chapter Four – Echo Chamber The classroom Orela led them to was small even by the school's original standards — low desks, scattered toys, cabinets with chipped paint. It looked ordinary enough.
